title: Explicit Teaching Isn't Regurgitation
author: Dr Nathaniel Swain
summary: Nathaniel Swain rebuts the common charge that explicit instruction produces passive, dependent learners, arguing instead that its purpose is generative rather than reproductive. He explains that novices lack the rich background knowledge experts rely on, so unguided discovery overloads working memory before students have anything to think with. Explicit teaching supplies that foundation through explanation, modelling, guided practice, and responsive feedback, which Swain frames not as a cage but as scaffolding that is progressively withdrawn as competence grows. He reframes the explicit-versus-inquiry debate as a question of sequencing rather than opposing philosophies, proposing a continuum running from explain through model, practise, apply, connect, generate, and investigate. The piece closes with the paradoxical goal at the heart of his argument: teachers explain clearly now so that students eventually need less explaining.
points: Reframes the explicit-instruction debate: the objection isn't whether inquiry belongs in the classroom but when and for what purpose it is introduced relative to a student's existing knowledge.
Ties the case to cognitive load theory, arguing that asking novices to discover concepts independently overloads working memory because they lack the expert schemas needed to manage the task.
Offers a concrete instructional sequence (explain, model, practise, apply, connect, generate, investigate) that treats explicit and inquiry-based methods as stages rather than rival ideologies.
Anchors the argument in his Read2Learn literacy work, where knowledge-rich explicit instruction fed into reading, writing, discussion, and hands-on application rather than rote reproduction.
quotes: One of the most persistent misconceptions about explicit teaching is that it produces passive learners: students who can reproduce what their teacher has told them, but struggle to think, question, create or explore for themselves.

When students are novices in a domain, they don't yet have the rich networks of knowledge that experts can draw upon. Asking them to independently discover important concepts or navigate complex problems can therefore place enormous demands on working memory.
This isn't about keeping students dependent on the teacher. It's about giving them the foundations from which independence can grow.

There should absolutely be opportunities for students to investigate, debate, solve problems, create, critique and pursue questions. But these experiences become much more productive when students bring sufficient knowledge and skill to them.
We don't explicitly teach because we want students to need explicit teaching forever. We explicitly teach so that they need even less explicit teaching earlier and earlier.
